Sergio, it is Marina. You are presenting the post-mortem on Tuesday, and I want three things in your head before you walk in. First, keep it blameless, and I mean the words as well as the intention. The moment you say a name in the same sentence as the word failure, the room stops listening to the system and starts watching the person, and you will never get the honest version of anything again. Say the step failed. Never say Camila failed. Second, the room will want to know what would have happened, so give them one counterfactual, and only one you can defend. If the alert had covered manual controls, we would have seen it on Monday afternoon. That one is true and you can prove it. Do not say we would have caught it in an hour, because you do not know that, and somebody in that room will ask you how. Third, and this is the one people get wrong. A post-mortem that ends in hindsight is a story. A post-mortem that ends in a change is work. So finish with the two changes, with a date on each one, and with your name on both. And one last thing. Call it a near miss out loud. If you call it a small issue, the committee will file it and forget it, and next quarter we will be having this conversation with a number that hurts.

Sergio, Paulo here, from the credit desk. Two minutes on how people actually talk in a post-mortem, because the grammar carries more meaning than you think. There are three sentences in that room and each one does a different job. Should have is the one with a finger in it. We should have named the deputy. That is criticism, and it is fine when you point it at your own desk, and it is a bad idea when you point it at somebody else's. Would have is the result. If the alert had covered manual controls, we would have seen it on Monday. No blame in that one, just a consequence, and that is exactly why the auditors like it. Might have is the honest one. We might have caught it earlier. You are saying it was possible, not certain, and when you do not know, that is the sentence that keeps you credible. Now the two mistakes I hear every week from good speakers. The first one is putting would in the if half. Never if we would have known. It is if we had known. The would lives in the other half of the sentence, always. The second one is smaller and it is everywhere. When you say it fast it sounds like would of, and some people write it that way. It is not of, it is have. Would have, should have, could have. Say them out loud a few times tonight and it will stop sounding wrong on Tuesday.

First, put the timeline on the table: what happened, and at what time. Then name the step that failed, never the person who was on duty. Next, trace the problem back to the one lapse that started it. After that, say what would have happened if the missing step had run. Finally, name the change, put a date on it, and put your name next to it.
